examples.label: CPTS Ch06 — full OpenVAS install + start
examples.command:
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get -y full-upgrade
sudo apt-get install -y gvm
sudo gvm-setup
sudo gvm-start
# Access https://127.0.0.1:9392

examples.label: Verify setup is correct after install

notes: Components: Greenbone Vulnerability Manager + Greenbone Security Assistant. Feeds: NVTs + CVEs. GVM (Greenbone Vulnerability Manager) is the open-source alternative to Nessus. gvm-setup takes 15-30 minutes on first run (downloads NVT/SCAP/CERT feeds). Admin password is printed at end of setup — save it. Web UI is at https://<ip>:9392 (port may vary). Also covered in: CPTS Ch06 (Vulnerability Assessment).
name: OpenVAS (GVM) - Install & Start
description: Install and initialize Greenbone Vulnerability Management (OpenVAS), the open-source scanner, then start it and log into the Greenbone Security Assistant web UI.

steps.label: 1. Install
steps.command:
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get -y full-upgrade
sudo apt-get install gvm

defense.why_it_works: OpenVAS (Greenbone GVM) is an open-source vulnerability scanner. It runs Network Vulnerability Tests (NVTs) that match discovered services/versions to known CVEs and perform active checks, producing a severity-rated findings report.
defense.prerequisites: GVM installed and network access to the target range. Authenticated scans additionally need valid host credentials.
defense.impact: A severity-rated vulnerability report across the target range for exploitation planning.
defense.detection: Same active-scan signature as any network scanner - a burst of probes across many hosts/ports. [MITRE T1595.002 AN1999] Monitor for anomalous traffic patterns and uncommon data flows; correlate with process/command-line monitoring. NVT traffic is IDS-recognisable.
defense.artifacts: A burst of connections across hosts/ports from the scanner IP; NVT request signatures; authenticated logons from the scanner if credentialed.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1595.002 M1056] Minimise exposed services/data; segment so only authorised scanners reach hosts; alert on scan bursts.
defense.evasion: Tune the scan config and schedule/throttle scans to reduce noise and rate-based detection.
defense.misconfiguration: Vulnerability scanning reveals services with unpatched CVEs, default configurations, or known-weak settings. The absence of a patch management process allows critical vulnerabilities to remain exploitable for months or years. Scan results that are not acted upon create a false sense of security.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# OpenVAS/Nessus finding typical vulnerable targets:
# CVSSv3: 9.8 - Apache Struts2 RCE (CVE-2017-5638) - unpatched
# CVSSv3: 8.8 - Tomcat manager with default creds (admin/admin)
# CVSSv3: 10.0 - MS17-010 (EternalBlue) - SMBv1 enabled, unpatched

# Unpatched = patch not applied within SLA:
# Critical (CVSS 9+): patch within 24-72 hours
# High (CVSS 7-8.9): patch within 7 days
# Medium: patch within 30 days
defense.secure_config:
# Establish a vulnerability management program:
# 1. Scan weekly with authenticated scans (Nessus/OpenVAS/Qualys)
# 2. Integrate scan results with ticketing (Jira/ServiceNow)
# 3. Set SLA by severity: Critical 72h, High 7d, Medium 30d
# 4. Verify patches with re-scan

# CVSS scoring -> risk-based prioritization:
# Not all CVSSv3 9+ are exploitable in your environment
# Use EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) to prioritize by actual exploitation likelihood

# Defense-in-depth: patch is the fix, but compensating controls while patching:
# WAF rule for web vuln CVEs
# Network segment to isolate vulnerable service
# IDS signature for exploit traffic
